title: The Effects of Police Violence on Inner-City Students
design_raw: Quasi-experimental dynamic difference-in-differences / event study with student fixed effects and neighborhood-semester fixed effects
causal_tier_reason: The workbook explicitly identifies a difference-in-differences design.
risk_of_bias_raw: Strong quasi-experimental design with rich spatial linkage and multiple robustness checks. Main limitations are possible residual time-varying hyperlocal confounding and use of last observed home address rather than complete residential histories.
exposure_window_raw: Objective geocoded police killings in Los Angeles County, 2002–2016; treatment within 0.50 miles, controls 0.50–3 miles.
outcomes: Primary proximal psychiatric/psychological outcome is emotional disturbance classification. Additional perceived-safety outcomes from School Experience Survey. Academic outcomes are GPA, absenteeism, graduation, and college enrollment.
outcome_measure: GPA; emotional disturbance classification; absenteeism; graduation; college enrollment; perceived safety survey items.
outcome_unit_scale: GPA points/SD; emotional disturbance per 1,000 students; absenteeism indicator; binary attainment outcomes.
effect_direction_raw: Deterioration: lower GPA, higher emotional disturbance classification, higher absenteeism, lower graduation/college enrollment.
statistically_significant_raw: Yes
effect_size_note: [NEEDS VERIFICATION] The source workbook does not provide a dedicated standardized effect-size field or separate confidence-interval bounds.
sample_size: 712,954 unique students” (LAUSD)
population_details: Gender: Not Reported. Student sample is 86% Black or Hispanic, 14% White or Asian. Police-killing decedents were 52% Hispanic, 26% Black, 19% White, 3% Asian, and 97% male.
data_source: LAUSD administrative student records linked to Los Angeles Times Homicide Database and district attorney incident reports
exposure_measure: Objective — geocoded distance from home to killing; treatment “within 0.50 miles,” control “between 0.50 and 3 miles.
mediators_mechanisms: Psychological trauma, perceived injustice, institutional distrust, safety perceptions, absenteeism disruption. Effects are larger for killings of Black/Hispanic individuals and for killings of unarmed individuals.
moderators: Student race/ethnicity, race of deceased, weapon status of deceased, grade of exposure, prior disadvantage.
finding_summary: Exposure to police killings increased absenteeism immediately after incidents, reduced GPA by roughly 0.07 to 0.08 points in the following semesters at peak, increased emotional disturbance classification by about 15% over baseline, and lowered high school graduation and college enrollment. Effects were concentrated among Black and Hispanic students and were largest for killings of unarmed individuals.
methodology: Hyperlocal spatial comparison plus staggered event timing. The design compares students who live very near killings with students in the same neighborhood who live slightly farther away, with student fixed effects, neighborhood-semester fixed effects, and cohort-year fixed effects.
estimand: DiD treatment effect for students living within 0.50 miles of police killings relative to 0.50–3 miles controls.
estimator: Dynamic DiD/event-study OLS with student fixed effects and neighborhood-semester fixed effects.
se_clustering: Clustered/robust SEs as specified by outcome; no IV first-stage.
outcome_timepoint: Immediate daily absenteeism; semester GPA/emotional disturbance; following-year perceived safety; long-run graduation/college enrollment.
missing_data_method: Administrative records; sample restrictions vary by outcome.
strengths_limitations: AMajor strengths are large administrative sample, exact geocoding, event-study validation, and multiple outcomes. Limits include generalizability beyond LAUSD and possible exposure misclassification from unobserved within-district moves.
policy_practice_implications: Police violence imposes educational and psychological spillovers on nearby youth, especially Black and Hispanic students, implying that use-of-force policy is an education and mental-health issue as well as a public-safety issue.
reviewer_notes: Design is DiD event-study with student and neighborhood-semester FE; GPA peak effect −0.07 to −0.08 at τ=1,2 (average posttreatment = −0.027); no pre-trends F=0.69, p=.655. All coding fields verified against full QJE source.

title: Local exposure to school shootings and youth antidepressant use
design_raw: Difference-in-Differences with event-study; month×year and school×area fixed effects
causal_tier_reason: The workbook explicitly identifies a difference-in-differences design.
risk_of_bias_raw: Low risk; robust quasi-experimental design: objective exposure (fatal school shootings), DiD with event-study showing no pre-trends, school-area and month×year fixed effects, enrollment-weighted near-universe pharmacy data, and multiple robustness/falsification checks; note the outcome measures prescribing, not symptoms.
exposure_window_raw: Providers 0–5 miles from affected school versus 10–15 miles reference; main post windows 2 and 3 years.
outcomes: Primary—monthly antidepressant prescriptions to youth (log count) and rates per 1,000. Adult antidepressants and youth opioids used as falsification outcomes.
outcome_measure: Monthly antidepressant prescriptions (log); also per-1,000
outcome_unit_scale: Log count; prescriptions per 1,000 youth.
effect_direction_raw: Deterioration (Increase in antidepressant prescriptions to youth under age 20)
statistically_significant_raw: Yes for fatal (p<.01); No for nonfatal.
effect_size_note: [NEEDS VERIFICATION] The source workbook does not provide a dedicated standardized effect-size field or separate confidence-interval bounds.
sample_size: 44 school shootings (15 fatal, 29 nonfatal); main tables report schools = 15 fatal / 29 nonfatal and observations ?1,412–2,718 depending on window (2y vs 3y).
population_details: Not a stratified outcome; descriptively, shooting schools had a higher share of Black students.
data_source: IQVIA Xponent pharmacy prescription data (near-universe); Washington Post school-shootings database; Census (populations); CDC provider counts; UCR crime; ACS insurance.
exposure_measure: Objective—date and location of school shootings; fatal vs nonfatal. Treatment area: providers 0–5 miles from the school; reference: 10–15 miles.
mediators_mechanisms: Not tested as formal mediators; authors interpret smaller effects where non-prescribing providers (psychologists/social workers) are denser as consistent with substitution toward behavioral care.
moderators: Fatal vs nonfatal; high school vs other levels (effects concentrated in high schools); local provider densities; robustness to alternative reference areas and distance bands.
finding_summary: Findings show that local exposure to fatal school shootings increases youth antidepressant use by 21.4% in the following 2 y. These effects are smaller in areas with a higher density of mental health providers who focus on behavioral, rather than pharmacological, intervention. Youth antidepressant use +21.3% (2 y) and +24.5% (3 y) in treatment areas relative to reference areas; increase appears within 6 months (~+30%) and persists ?2 y. Nonfatal shootings: null. Effects larger in high schools. Effects are smaller where non-prescribing providers are denser; no change in adult antidepressants or youth opioids.
methodology: DiD comparing 0–5 mi vs 10–15 mi before/after; month×year and school×area FE. Event-study shows no pre-trends; robustness with alternative reference areas, distance definitions, and wild-cluster bootstrap.
estimand: DiD ATT for treated areas (area-level).
estimator: OLS DiD with month-by-year and school-by-area fixed effects.
se_clustering: Clustered at school-by-area level; wild-cluster bootstrap in robustness checks.
outcome_timepoint: Effects emerge within months and persist for approximately 2–3 years.
missing_data_method: School-area months included under prescription-count selection rule; no imputation noted.
strengths_limitations: Strengths: near-universe RX data; objective exposure timing; strong FE structure; clean event-study pre-trend; falsification (adults/opioids). Limitations: prescriptions capture treatment, not prevalence; cannot partition incidence vs treatment of existing cases; heterogeneity by provider density relies on 12 counties.
policy_practice_implications: Expect sustained increases in mental-health treatment demand after fatal school shootings; bolster non-pharmacological resources (psychology/social work) locally, which correlate with smaller RX spikes.
reviewer_notes: Keep the fatal vs nonfatal distinction explicit. Pair this study with day-scale sleep/attention papers for acute effects; this one is months–years and prescriptions.

title: Surviving a mass shooting
age_range: Ages 14-18 at the event (middle-school survivors 14-15; high-school survivors 14-18).
design_raw: Matched difference-in-differences (DiD); individual fixed effects for health outcomes; matched treatment–control comparisons for medium-term outcomes.
causal_tier_reason: The workbook explicitly identifies a difference-in-differences design.
risk_of_bias_raw: Low risk given national admin data, precise exposure, matched DiD with clear pre-trends for school outcomes; medium-term outcomes rely on matched comparisons without pre-period.
exposure_window_raw: Survivorship of Utøya attack (Hole municipality) on July 22, 2011; survivors from municipalities nationwide.
outcomes: Psychological diagnosis indicator (ICPC-2 P01–P99 / ICD-10) and number of GP visits. Related educational outcomes (school performance/attainment) also central: GPA, exam scores, on-time completion, HS diploma, higher-ed enrollment/completion.
outcome_measure: Administrative registers—GPA/exam scores, GP visits, psychological diagnoses, employment/earnings.
outcome_unit_scale: GPA and exam scores standardized by cohort (SD units); completion/diploma/enrollment probabilities; count of GP visits; binary diagnosis indicator; employment indicator; log earnings.
effect_direction_raw: Adverse (higher diagnoses; lower GPA/attainment).
statistically_significant_raw: Yes (GPA, on-time completion, GP visits, psychological diagnosis).
effect_size_note: [NEEDS VERIFICATION] The source workbook does not provide a dedicated standardized effect-size field or separate confidence-interval bounds.
sample_size: All middle- and high-school-aged children who survived the Utoya, July 22, 2011 mass shooting; matched controls; survivors parents and siblings; same-aged school peers.
population_details: Mixed gender; race/ethnicity not reported (Norway administrative data).
data_source: Linked national administrative registers (Norwegian Police Directorate victim registry; school registers; KUHR health claims; tax and employer–employee records).
exposure_measure: Objective—identified as survivors of attempted murder in July 2011 in Hole municipality (Utøya).
mediators_mechanisms: Not tested formally; paper discusses immediate and persistent health-care utilization and diagnoses as channels; notes large parental responses (sickness leave, diagnoses).
moderators: Spillovers reported separately for mothers, fathers, siblings; peers overall and by peer gender; results shown by cohort (age at event)
finding_summary: findings show that in the short run children who survive have substantially lower GPA (nearly 0.5 SD) and increased utilization of health care services and more mental health diagnoses. In the medium run, survivors have fewer years of schooling completed and lower labor force participation. Parents and siblings of survivors are also impacted, experiencing substantial increases in doctor visits and mental health diagnoses. However, there appear to be limited impacts on school aged peers of survivors. While this event affected the entire country, we show that survivors and their families bear significant costs despite robust social safety nets and universal access to healthcare. Short-run (school year immediately after): Middle-school GPA ?0.527 SD (p<.01); exam scores ?0.326 SD (ns). High-school on-time completion ?0.189 and ?0.213 (probability) for 1st and 3rd grade, respectively (both p<.01). GP visits +0.644 (from ?1.06 baseline) and psychological diagnosis +0.367 (?+36 pp from ?10% base) (both p<.01). Medium-run (by 2018): HS diploma ?0.129, ever higher-ed enrollment ?0.0712, ever higher-ed completion ?0.0638 (all pp; all significant). Employment ?0.0489 pp (p<.05). Log earnings ?0.133 (ns). Family spillovers: Mothers—sickness leave +0.0671, GP visits +0.474, psychological diagnosis +0.142 (all p<.01). Fathers—GP visits +0.171, psychological diagnosis +0.0743 (p<.01). Siblings—exam scores ?0.227 SD, GPA ?0.220 SD (both p<.10), psychological diagnosis +0.0311 (p<.01). Peers: largely muted; small significant negatives for female peers on exam scores (?0.161 SD) and small increase in diagnoses (+0.0140).
methodology: Coarsened Exact Matching to create survivor–control pairs plus DiD leveraging pre/post timing; individual fixed effects for health outcomes; for medium-term outcomes, matched treatment–control difference (no pre-period available).
estimand: ATT for survivors (via matched DiD / matched differences).
estimator: DiD with matched controls and controls for gender/parental SES/centrality; individual fixed effects for health; matched differences for medium-term.
se_clustering: School outcomes clustered at school-cohort; survivors’ health robust SEs; family outcomes clustered on mother ID.
outcome_timepoint: Short-run 2011–2013 for school; health annually 2006–2016; medium-run education and labor outcomes measured by 2018.
missing_data_method: Matching included categories for missing parental variables; otherwise not highlighted as an issue
strengths_limitations: Strengths: Population-wide registers; objective exposure; rich outcomes across survivors, family, peers; fixed-effects health models; explicit cohort timing. Limitations: Unique event with extensive state support; some outcomes lack pre-period (medium-run); external validity cautioned by authors.
policy_practice_implications: Survivors and families bear substantial educational and mental-health costs even with universal health care; need for sustained post-event supports for youths and families.
reviewer_notes: Authors show pre-2011 lines are flat for school outcomes and sharp post-event drops; health impacts are immediate and persist ?5 years; peer effects minimal.

title: Children’s Cognitive Performance and Selective Attention Following Recent Community Violence
design_raw: quasi-experimental fixed-effects design.
causal_tier_reason: The workbook does not clearly document an RCT, DiD, natural experiment, IV, within-person fixed-effects, or within-family fixed-effects design.
risk_of_bias_raw: Lower Risk: Strong internal validity via fixed-effects strategy and exogenous variation in crime timing; some sample attrition.
exposure_window_raw: Police-reported violent crime within 0.5 mile and 7 days before assessment; tighter windows used in sensitivity analyses.
outcomes: Cognitive performance (reaction time, accuracy), selective attention to emotional stimuli
outcome_measure: Dot-probe task: average response time (milliseconds) as primary cognitive-performance outcome; accuracy and attention-bias/facilitation scores as secondary outcomes.
outcome_unit_scale: Milliseconds; proportion correct; facilitation/attention-bias measures.
effect_direction_raw: Mixed acute cognitive pattern: faster response time, marginally lower accuracy, and anxiety-dependent attention patterns.
statistically_significant_raw: Yes for response time; accuracy is marginal; selected anxiety interactions significant.
effect_size_note: [NEEDS VERIFICATION] The source workbook does not provide a dedicated standardized effect-size field or separate confidence-interval bounds.
sample_size: 359 children
population_details: 46.5% boys; 70.5% Black, 24.2% Hispanic, 5.3% White/Other
data_source: Chicago School Readiness Project, Chicago Police Department crime data
exposure_measure: Objective – geocoded police-reported violent crimes within proximity/time
mediators_mechanisms: Biobehavioral stress response, trait anxiety
moderators: Trait anxiety
finding_summary: Children exposed to recent violence showed faster but marginally less accurate cognitive responses. Trait anxiety moderated the effect: low-anxiety children showed vigilant patterns, high-anxiety children showed avoidant patterns. Children assessed within 7 days of a violent crime within ½ mile showed faster dot-probe responses (b = ?17.18 ms, SE = 6.10, p < .01) and were marginally less accurate (b = ?0.002, SE = .001, p < .10) than peers assessed outside that window; there were no overall effects on selective attention. Effects varied by trait anxiety: the treatment × anxiety interaction predicted average response time (b = 33.49, SE = 14.36, p < .05) and positive facilitation (b = 14.69, SE = 7.08, p < .05). Simple slopes showed low-anxiety children were faster when recently exposed (b = ?28.53, SE = 7.96, p < .01), while high-anxiety children were not (b = ?4.65, SE = 7.85, p = .75). For selective attention to positive images, high-anxiety children showed more attention toward positive stimuli (b = 7.50, SE = 3.89, p < .10, marginal), whereas low-anxiety children showed less (b = ?2.89, SE = 3.61, p = .22). Using a tighter window (within ¼ mile and assessed more recently), the anxiety × treatment interaction for negative facilitation was significant (b = ?42.74, SE = 20.86, p < .05); the simple slope for high-anxiety was null (b = ?9.28, SE = 14.56, p = .75), while low-anxiety children showed greater attention toward negative stimuli (b = 20.93, SE = 9.99, p < .05).
methodology: Radial fixed effects comparing treated vs control assessments by timing/proximity of violent events
estimand: Acute treatment contrast for children assessed after recent nearby violent crime versus controls outside the window.
estimator: Fixed-effects regression using radial/proximity-time exposure indicators.
se_clustering: Adjusted for repeated observations/person-crime structure as reported.
outcome_timepoint: Same assessment week, within 7 days of exposure.
missing_data_method: Listwise/complete-case analytic sample after follow-up restrictions.
strengths_limitations: Strengths: Novel within-neighborhood design, objective crime data, trait anxiety moderation. Limitations: No long-term outcomes, subsample attrition (~60% follow-up), potential residual confounding.
policy_practice_implications: Acute community violence impacts cognitive functioning; mental health interventions should consider differential susceptibility by trait anxiety.
reviewer_notes: Tightly designed quasi-experiment; unique contribution to mental health and neurocognition literature; indirect proxy for mental health effects.

title: The Consequences of High-Fatality School Shootings for Surviving Students
age_range: School-aged children and adolescents; Columbine mortality analysis follows survivors to age 30. Exact age range varies by sub-analysis
design_raw: Difference-in-differences with event-study models
causal_tier_reason: The workbook explicitly identifies a difference-in-differences design.
risk_of_bias_raw: Low: Authors note some evidence of differential pre-trends in parts of the Sandy Hook test score analysis, though generally wrong-signed relative to the post-shooting decline. They also note reliance on aggregated school-level or county-level data, lack of individual test-score tracking in some analyses, and inability to directly compare high- vs low-fatality magnitudes econometrically in the final paper
exposure_window_raw: Exposure is the occurrence of a high-fatality school shooting at the school or district. Temporal windows vary by case study and available data
outcomes: The paper does not use direct symptom scales. Outcomes are educational record, chronic absenteeism, and mortality including suicide and accidental poisonings/overdoses. For your template, these are better treated as downstream or indirect consequences rather than direct mental health symptom outcomes
outcome_measure: Standardized test scores, proficiency rate percentiles, chronic absenteeism rate, and cause-specific mortality records
outcome_unit_scale: Test scores in standard deviation units in SEDA; proficiency percentile ranks for Connecticut school-level test data; chronic absenteeism percentage points; mortality rates and derived counts in the Columbine analysis
effect_direction_raw: Harmful. Lower test performance, higher absenteeism, and worse mortality outcomes
statistically_significant_raw: Yes for key reported outcomes
effect_size_note: [NEEDS VERIFICATION] The source workbook does not provide a dedicated standardized effect-size field or separate confidence-interval bounds.
sample_size: Varies by analysis. For Sandy Hook school-level proficiency analysis, sample size was 3,726 for math proficiency percentile, 3,726 for ELA proficiency percentile, and 1,876 for chronic absenteeism. For district-level Sandy Hook standardized test score analysis, one visible table reports sample sizes of 6,788, 6,776, and 2,327 for selected outcomes. No single overall study N is reported because the paper uses multiple datasets and analytic samples
population_details: Mortality data include age, sex, and race/ethnicity, but the paper does not present one unified study sample composition across all analyses
data_source: Stanford Education Data Archive for Sandy Hook district test scores; Connecticut school-level data for Sandy Hook school test scores and chronic absenteeism; Florida state data for Parkland test scores; Vital Statistics Multiple Cause-of-Death Mortality data for Columbine
exposure_measure: Objective. High-fatality school shootings at Columbine, Sandy Hook, and Parkland
mediators_mechanisms: NR as tested mediators. The paper discusses trauma and school disruption conceptually
moderators: Sex in Columbine mortality analyses; spillovers to other schools in the same district are also examined
finding_summary: High-fatality shootings led to substantial reductions in attendance and test scores. Sandy Hook chronic absenteeism increased by 1.94 percentage points in DiD models; the first full post-shooting year effect was 4.14 percentage points in the event-study table. Sandy Hook math and ELA proficiency percentile fell by 18.14 and 16.75 points, respectively, at the affected school. The paper reports Columbine survivors were more likely to die by age 30, especially boys, with higher suicide and accidental poisoning/overdose mortality
methodology: Difference-in-differences comparing affected schools to other schools in the same state before and after the shooting, with school and year fixed effects. Event-study models were used to examine pre-trends and post-shooting dynamics. Regressions were weighted by school enrollment; standard errors were clustered at the school level in the general framework, and at the district level in the Sandy Hook school-level table notes
estimand: NR
estimator: Difference-in-differences and event-study regressions
se_clustering: General framework states clustering at school level; Sandy Hook Table 2 notes clustering at district level
outcome_timepoint: Short-run and longer-run post-shooting periods; Columbine mortality tracked through young adulthood
missing_data_method: Not a single unified method. For some Connecticut school-level proficiency analyses, suppressed values were imputed using an assumed value of five to maintain a full panel; for absenteeism, bottom-coded missing rates were replaced with the lowest observed percentage in other years to maintain a balanced panel, with sensitivity checks omitting those observations

policy_practice_implications: Supports school-based trauma response, attendance support, academic remediation, and long-run survivor monitoring after high-fatality shootings
reviewer_notes: strong quasi-experimental design focused on downstream consequences of trauma exposure (educational performance, absenteeism, and mortality); the study does not directly measure mental health symptoms but examines outcomes plausibly influenced by trauma

title: The Acute Effect of Local Homicides on Children’s Cognitive Performance.
design_raw: Natural experiment (quasi-experimental design exploiting timing of violent events with fixed-effects)
causal_tier_reason: The workbook explicitly identifies a natural experiment.
risk_of_bias_raw: Low: The study’s internal validity is strengthened by the fixed-effects strategy, which addresses selection bias by holding constant all time-invariant neighborhood factors
exposure_window_raw: A local homicide in the child’s immediate neighborhood – analyzed at multiple geographic scales (within the child’s census block group, and also at the broader census tract and neighborhood-cluster levels). Temporal: Recent exposure defined acutely – typically a homicide occurring within approximately one week prior to the child’s assessment date. (Analyses indicate the impact is strongest for homicides very close in time to the test and diminishes as the time gap increases beyond a week.)
outcomes: Children’s cognitive performance on standardized tests (vocabulary and reading achievement scores)
outcome_measure: Standardized cognitive assessments – specifically, a vocabulary test from the WISC-R (Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children – Revised) and a reading achievement test (Wide Range Achievement Test, WRAT-3) in the PHDCN sample. In the replication sample, outcomes were the Woodcock-Johnson Letter-Word Identification test (reading) and Woodcock-Johnson Applied Problems test (math)
outcome_unit_scale: Test score units (standardized assessments). Effects are reported in standard deviation units (~0.5–0.66 SD drop associated with homicide exposure). (For reference, many of these tests have a population mean ~100, SD ~15, so a 0.5 SD decline is on the order of 7–8 points on an IQ or achievement scale, indicating a substantively meaningful drop.)
effect_direction_raw: Negative – exposure to a local homicide had an adverse impact, lowering children’s cognitive test scores (i.e., violence exposure → worse performance)
statistically_significant_raw: Yes. The decline in scores for children assessed within ~1 week of a nearby homicide was statistically significant (e.g., roughly half to two-thirds of a standard deviation decrease, with p-values < .05 for key comparisons)
effect_size_note: [NEEDS VERIFICATION] The source workbook does not provide a dedicated standardized effect-size field or separate confidence-interval bounds.
sample_size: 1,082 children (2,294 cognitive assessments) in main sample; replication sample 180 children (348 assessments)
population_details: Predominantly African-American and Hispanic children; analyses conducted separately by race (effect observed among Black/African-American children, not significant for Hispanic children)
data_source: Project on Human Development in Chicago Neighborhoods (PHDCN) child sample (1994–2002) merged with Chicago Police Department homicide records; plus a replication using Chicago data from the Three City Study of Welfare, Children and Families
exposure_measure: Objective – exposure to a local homicide event (police-reported homicide in child’s neighborhood)
mediators_mechanisms: No mediators directly measured. Authors suggest that acute stress responses (e.g. psychological distress in the aftermath of violence) likely impair children’s attention and self-regulation, explaining the cognitive performance drop
moderators: Race/ethnicity functioned as a moderator – the acute negative effect was significant for African-American children, whereas no significant effect was detected for Hispanic children. (No other moderators like age, gender, family factors were reported.)
finding_summary: When a child’s assessment took place within roughly a week after a homicide occurred near their home, the child’s cognitive test scores were significantly lower. Specifically, exposure to a local homicide <1 week prior was associated with ~0.5 to 0.66 standard deviation reductions in vocabulary and reading scores. These acute effects were observed among Black children and appeared to dissipate after about 7–10 days (no lasting impact beyond the immediate week). No significant short-term impact was found for Hispanic children. The main result was replicated in an independent Chicago sample, confirming that extreme local violence has a community-wide acute effect on children’s cognitive performance even if they are not direct witnesses
methodology: Exploits ostensibly random timing of local homicide events relative to scheduled child assessments. The analysis compares children in the same neighborhood and survey wave who were assessed shortly after a homicide versus those assessed at other times, using fixed effects to control for all stable neighborhood characteristics. In practice, a linear regression with tract-by-wave fixed effects and calendar time controls (month and year) was used, so the effect is identified by within-neighborhood, within-period variation in exposure timing. This approach is intended to isolate the causal impact of the homicide event by differencing out between-neighborhood differences and seasonal trends.
estimand: Average Treatment Effect (ATE) – the analysis estimates the average causal effect of a recent local homicide on children’s cognitive test performance in the sample (contrast between being exposed vs not exposed in the week before assessment)
estimator: OLS regression with fixed effects. The primary estimator was a linear regression of test scores on an indicator for a recent local homicide, including tract-by-wave fixed effects to control for neighborhood and cohort factors, and month/year fixed effects to control for seasonality. This yields a difference-in-differences-like estimate based on within-neighborhood, within-time-frame comparisons. Robust standard errors were used to determine significance (see next item).
se_clustering: Not explicitly reported in the paper. (Given the design, the analysis likely used robust standard errors clustered at a neighborhood level to account for non-independence of observations within the same community. The reported significance levels. suggest that appropriate clustering or adjustment was applied, though the article does not state the exact clustering unit.)
outcome_timepoint: Acute/short-term – children’s cognitive outcomes were measured at the time of the scheduled assessment, which for the “exposed” group was in the immediate aftermath of a local homicide (within days up to one week after the incident). There was no long-term follow-up in this study beyond the initial assessment window.
missing_data_method: Not reported. The study did not describe handling of missing data, implying that analyses were likely based on cases with complete data (listwise deletion).
multiple_testing_adjustment: None reported. (The paper examined multiple outcome measures but did not mention any adjustment for multiple comparisons, likely focusing on conceptually related outcomes of cognitive performance without formal correction.)
strengths_limitations: Strengths: Innovative natural experiment design using real-world violence timing, with rigorous fixed-effects controls for neighborhood context. Uses objective crime data and standardized cognitive assessments, and the main findings were replicated in a second independent sample, bolstering confidence in the results. Limitations: The effect is short-lived and measured only in the acute term, so longer-term impacts on mental health or academics were not assessed. The null finding for Hispanic children raises questions about generalizability or suggests unmeasured differences (mechanisms may differ by subgroup). The study is observational; although timing is treated as random, there is no true randomization, and results could be affected if, for instance, interview scheduling or attendance was influenced by the violence (not examined). No direct data on potential mediating processes (e.g. child’s emotional state or caregiver reactions) were collected, which limits understanding of the causal pathway.
policy_practice_implications: This research suggests that community violence can have immediate detrimental effects on children’s cognitive functioning, even among those not personally victimized. Therefore, policies aimed at violence reduction and rapid post-violence support could have educational and developmental benefits. The authors highlight the need for broader recognition that extreme violent events reverberate across the whole community’s children. In practice, this could mean providing counseling or academic accommodations for children in the aftermath of local traumatic events, and treating community violence prevention as part of improving educational outcomes. It also implies that high-stakes testing and evaluations of children might need to account for recent trauma exposure (since test performance may temporarily drop following nearby homicides).

title: Local Homicide and Children’s Cognitive Performance
design_raw: Fixed-effects panel design using longitudinal Mexican Family Life Survey data with within-child and within-community variation in homicide exposure.
causal_tier_reason: The workbook explicitly identifies a within-person fixed-effects comparison.
risk_of_bias_raw: Low: Study documents data quality of MxFLS, high follow-up rates, and robustness checks. Remaining risk arises from potential time-varying confounders and measurement error in homicide counts.
exposure_window_raw: Spatial. Municipality of residence (MxFLS community). Temporal. Homicides occurring in windows before the child’s test date, with attention to recent and prior exposure windows as defined in the paper.
outcomes: Primary outcome is cognitive performance: percent correct responses on Raven’s Progressive Matrices.
outcome_measure: Raven’s Progressive Matrices (non-verbal cognitive test).
outcome_unit_scale: Percentage of correct Raven’s items (0–100%).
effect_direction_raw: Mixed. Near-zero or small effects for children without prior exposure. Among children with prior exposure, additional homicides are associated with higher Raven scores in several models.
statistically_significant_raw: Yes for several key coefficients. The paper reports statistically significant estimates for homicide exposure among previously exposed children in main models.
effect_size_note: [NEEDS VERIFICATION] The source workbook does not provide a dedicated standardized effect-size field or separate confidence-interval bounds.
sample_size: 10,203 child-wave observations. 4,587 observations without prior municipal homicide exposure and 5,616 with prior exposure (after exclusions).
population_details: Sample includes boys and girls. Study reports indicators for indigenous status and other sociodemographic variables, but not detailed racial breakdowns beyond indigenous vs non-indigenous categories.
data_source: Mexican Family Life Survey (MxFLS) waves 1–3 for child and household data, combined with homicide counts from Mexican administrative sources (Data Cívica and related official data).
exposure_measure: Objective. Number of homicides in the child’s municipality within specified temporal windows before the cognitive assessment, based on official homicide records.
mediators_mechanisms: No formal mediation models estimated. Paper discusses possible mechanisms such as stress, vigilance, and adaptation as narrative interpretation.
moderators: Key moderator. Prior exposure to homicides in the child’s municipality (children with and without prior exposure, and varying levels of prior exposure). Age, sex, and other sociodemographic variables serve as controls; heterogeneity by prior exposure is central.
finding_summary: For children with no previous homicide exposure, recent local homicides have small or null effects on cognitive performance. For children with prior exposure, additional homicides before testing are associated with higher cognitive scores in some specifications, consistent with an interpretation of heightened vigilance and possible adaptation. The magnitude and direction of estimated effects depend on prior exposure levels and model specification; the paper emphasizes that repeated exposure may alter the impact of violence on cognition.
methodology: Use panel structure of MxFLS to estimate child-level models with fixed effects that absorb all time-invariant individual and community characteristics. Exploit temporal and spatial variation in municipal homicide rates around test dates, include wave/year and month fixed effects as well as a rich set of time-varying controls. Authors discuss remaining concerns around time-varying confounding and selection.
estimand: Not explicitly labeled. Estimated coefficients represent within-child average effects of changes in municipal homicide rates on cognitive scores over time.
estimator: Linear regression with child fixed effects, wave/year and month fixed effects, and additional controls, estimated on panel data.
se_clustering: Standard errors clustered at the municipality level (as reported in the methods and table notes).
outcome_timepoint: Cognitive test at survey interview date, after defined homicide exposure windows.
missing_data_method: The analytic sample excludes observations with missing key variables; no imputation procedure is described. Mark as “listwise deletion/complete case” based on this description.
strengths_limitations: Strengths. Nationally representative longitudinal data, repeated cognitive measures, linkage to objective violence data, and fixed-effects strategy with rich temporal controls. Limitations. Cognitive, not mental health outcomes. Municipal-level homicide exposure may not capture micro-level exposure. Authors note that adaptation and selection could complicate causal interpretation.
policy_practice_implications: Study suggests that violence exposure does not uniformly harm cognition. In heavily affected settings, repeated exposure might produce complex adaptations. Authors call for nuanced policy responses that address both psychological and cognitive consequences of chronic violence and caution against assuming universal detrimental effects.
reviewer_notes: Age range overlaps your 10–29 criterion via 10–14 subset, though sample includes 5–9 year olds. Outcome is cognitive, related to your cognitive-performance strand.

title: The effect of cumulative childhood exposure to neighbourhood socioeconomic disadvantage on school performance. a register-based study on neighbourhoods, schools, and siblings
design_raw: Fixed-effects design using siblings within multilevel models, plus variance partitioning by neighbourhood, school, and family. Quasi-experimental sibling comparison.
causal_tier_reason: The workbook explicitly identifies a within-family sibling or twin comparison.
risk_of_bias_raw: Low: High-quality administrative data covering the total population of urban cohorts, with annual residential histories and neighbourhood measures across childhood. Sibling design that accounts for all time-invariant shared family factors, plus adjustment for time-varying family covariates. Limitations they emphasise. Modest neighbourhood variation in Finland and relatively low segregation, which may limit power to detect neighbourhood effects. Use of postal codes as neighbourhoods may be imperfect for some questions, although the authors defend suitability in this context. For your coding you could mark overall risk of bias as low–moderate for selection and confounding, with some concerns about generalisability to more segregated settings.
exposure_window_raw: Spatial unit. Postal-code areas, mean population ≈ 4,728; median area size 3.4 km², interpreted by authors as small enough to be perceived as neighbourhoods. Temporal window. Ages 0–15. Cumulative exposure constructed as duration-weighted mean deprivation during childhood and adolescence and for sub-periods 0–6, 7–12, 13–15.
outcomes: Primary outcome is educational. grade point average (GPA) at end of compulsory school.
outcome_measure: GPA over 11–13 subjects, numeric scale 4–10.
outcome_unit_scale: GPA over 11–13 subjects, numeric scale 4–10
effect_direction_raw: Neighbourhood deprivation → GPA. Direction. Null overall, with a small adverse effect among children of parents with basic education that is not statistically significant.
statistically_significant_raw: No. Authors explicitly state “we observed no effect,” and the effect among low-education families is “not statistically significant.”
effect_size_note: [NEEDS VERIFICATION] The source workbook does not provide a dedicated standardized effect-size field or separate confidence-interval bounds.
sample_size: Initial study population. 103,861 children in 74,222 families, residing in 299 postal-code areas and attending 260 schools. Sibling analytic sample. 59,240 siblings in 27,095 families, residing in 298 postal-code areas and attending 260 schools.
population_details: Sex (girls vs boys) included as an individual-level covariate. Race/ethnicity not reported. Population is the total population of Finnish children living in major cities.
data_source: Linked Finnish administrative registers compiled by Statistics Finland, including: Total population register of children aged 0–14 in 2000 linked to biological parents and households. Register on applications to secondary-level education (for GPA and school identifiers). Yearly individual-level sociodemographic register used to derive postal-code area characteristics from 1987–2011.
exposure_measure: Objective: Cumulative neighbourhood socioeconomic disadvantage. Operationalised as a deprivation index at postal-code level, built from unemployment rate and proportions of adults (18–64) in lowest income quintile, manual workers, and welfare recipients in each year and area. Principal component analysis produced a standardized deprivation index for each year and postal-code area. Individual exposure is the duration-weighted mean of the index from ages 0–15 and separately for 0–6, 7–12, 13–15. Type. Objective, register-based
mediators_mechanisms: None specified as formal mediators; study decomposes variance attributable to neighbourhood, school, and family without testing mediation pathways
moderators: No formal moderator analyses reported; parental education subgroup examined in robustness checks quality, and neighbourhood conditions as mechanisms conceptually
finding_summary: Overall, after accounting for observed and unobserved family characteristics using the sibling design, the study finds no effect of neighbourhood socioeconomic disadvantage on GPA in the general population. Among children of parents with only basic education, there is a non-negligible but statistically non-significant effect of neighbourhood disadvantage on GPA. Family factors account for most of the variation in GPA, while only about 1 percent of variance is attributable to the neighbourhood and a small share to schools.
methodology: Sibling design that compares siblings within the same family who differ in their cumulative exposure to neighbourhood deprivation over ages 0–15. This comparison removes all time-invariant shared family characteristics, including those that drive sorting into neighbourhoods. Multilevel models with random intercepts for family, school, and neighbourhood, decomposing variation and exposure into between- and within-family components. Adjusts for time-varying family characteristics (e.g., household income, parental unemployment, parental separation, moves) measured over ages 0–15 and sub-periods.
estimand: Not labelled in the paper. In your sheet I would mark this as “NR (not specified).
estimator: Multilevel linear models with random intercepts for family, school, and neighbourhood. Sibling fixed-effects component by decomposing neighbourhood exposure into within-family and between-family parts.
se_clustering: Standard errors arise from the multilevel structure with random intercepts at family, school, and neighbourhood levels. The paper does not mention separate cluster-robust variance estimation. I would code “NR; multilevel random-effects SEs.
outcome_timepoint: GPA at end of compulsory school, 9th grade, age 15–16.
missing_data_method: Children who moved out of the nine large cities between ages 0 and 15 were excluded. Children without GPA because they did not apply to secondary education were excluded (2.3 percent). Children in very small schools (≤10 students) were excluded (0.2 percent).
strengths_limitations: Strengths. total-population register data, strong sibling design, long exposure window, explicit decomposition of variance across family, school, and neighbourhood. Limitations. only educational outcomes, relatively low neighbourhood inequality, no direct mental health measures.
policy_practice_implications: Authors argue that the very small neighbourhood contribution and strong family and school effects may reflect successful Finnish educational and social policies that limit the emergence of neighbourhood effects on schooling.
reviewer_notes: No mental health outcome, only GPA. It will not meet your 10–29 mental health inclusion criterion but is relevant context for neighbourhood-education discussions. • Strong example of sibling FE in a low-segregation welfare state, useful for comparison to US studies.

title: Using Fixed-Effects Analyses to Examine How Neighborhood Structural, Process, and Physical Characteristics Predict Children’s Cognitive Skills in a National Cohort of Elementary School Students
age_range: Children followed from kindergarten entry in 2010–2011 through fifth grade. mean age 101.35 months (SD 20.83). minimum and maximum ages NR
design_raw: Fixed-effects (FE) longitudinal panel. child fixed-effects regression exploiting within-child changes in neighborhood conditions over time
causal_tier_reason: The workbook explicitly identifies a within-person fixed-effects comparison.
risk_of_bias_raw: Low: Fixed-effects approach reduces selection bias from time-invariant confounders; large nationally representative cohort; multiple imputation; survey weights applied robust clustered SEs, survey weights, multiple imputation. Limitations. no mental health outcome, possible residual time-varying confounding, limited within-child variation for green space, no explicit multiple-testing control.
exposure_window_raw: Annual neighborhood measures from 2011–2016 matched to residence; crime and learning resources at ZIP-code level; other measures at census-tract level.
outcomes: Academic skills (reading, math IRT scores) and executive functions (DCCS and WJ-III Numbers Reversed composite)
outcome_measure: Reading and math IRT-based assessments; executive functions measured with DCCS and Woodcock-Johnson III Numbers Reversed composite.
outcome_unit_scale: Reading/math IRT common scale; executive-function standardized composite, mean 0, SD 1.
effect_direction_raw: Deterioration for violent crime and pollution on academic skills; improvement for learning resources, school quality, and green space; limited EF effects.
statistically_significant_raw: Yes for several academic-skill predictors; limited significant EF predictors.
effect_size_note: [NEEDS VERIFICATION] The source workbook does not provide a dedicated standardized effect-size field or separate confidence-interval bounds.
sample_size: Approximately 13,550 children with a valid spring-kindergarten weight. NCES requires Ns to be rounded to the nearest 50
population_details: About 52% male. racial/ethnic composition. 53% White, 26% Latinx, 12% Black, 5% Asian, 1% Pacific Islander/Native American, 4% multiracial
data_source: Early Childhood Longitudinal Study – Kindergarten Class of 2010–2011 (ECLS-K:2011), sponsored by NCES. geocoded home residence each year linked to multiple administrative neighborhood data sources (ACS, UCR, Zip Code Business Patterns, Child Opportunity Index, EPA RSEI, CDC National Landcover Database)
exposure_measure: Seven objective neighborhood characteristics, all area-level measures: Concentrated disadvantage. composite of percent in poverty, public assistance, unemployed, without high school degree, female-headed households from ACS 5-year estimates, standardized and averaged (α = .92). Violent crime. log of annual summed counts of murder, manslaughter, assault, rape, robbery from FBI UCR, aggregated to zip code, then averaged across zip codes within 2-mile radius of child’s zip-code centroid. Learning resources. log of annual counts of educational and cultural establishments (e.g., early childhood centers, schools, tutoring services, museums, libraries, zoos) from Zip Code Business Patterns at zip-code level. School-level achievement. census-tract level mean percentage of third graders proficient in math and reading on NAEP based on Child Opportunity Index data, reading and math averaged because r = .91. School-level AP course enrollment. proportion of 11th–12th grade students taking at least one AP course, from Civil Rights Data Collection via Child Opportunity Index. Green space. inverse of percentage of census tract covered by impervious surfaces, from CDC National Landcover Database (2011 only) matched to census tract across all waves. Pollution. EPA Risk-Screening Environmental Indicator (RSEI) score for census tract (air, water, soil toxic releases), 2010 and 2015 values interpolated/extrapolated to match study years
mediators_mechanisms: No formal mediators estimated; study framed by Leventhal and Dupéré integrated model linking structural, process, and physical neighborhood features to child development
moderators: No moderator analyses reported in main models
finding_summary: Longitudinal child fixed-effects regression (xtreg, fe) predicting within-child change in cognitive scores from within-child change in neighborhood characteristics, while controlling for time-varying covariates (child age, maternal education, household income, marital status, number of children, non-English home language, move between waves). Robust standard errors clustered at the child level using vce(cluster CHILDID)
methodology: Child fixed-effects regression exploiting within-child changes in neighborhood conditions over time; compares same child across years with different neighborhood exposures; controls for time-varying covariates
estimand: NR — within-child FE association, not explicitly named causal estimand.
estimator: Linear child fixed-effects regression estimated with Stata xtreg, fe.
se_clustering: Robust standard errors clustered at child level.
outcome_timepoint: Repeated spring-wave outcomes from kindergarten through fifth grade; contemporaneous within-child change models.
missing_data_method: Multiple imputation by chained equations; 30 imputed datasets; children without geographic identifier dropped for that wave.
strengths_limitations: Strengths: nationally representative ECLS-K:2011 cohort; repeated direct cognitive assessments; seven objective neighborhood measures; child FE with robust clustered SEs; survey weights; multiple imputation. Limitations: no mental health outcome; observational design cannot control all time-varying confounders; limited within-child variation for green space; no explicit multiple-testing control. achievement, and emphasize pollution, violent crime, school quality, learning resources, and green space as promising targets
policy_practice_implications: Improving neighborhood structural conditions (reducing crime and pollution), process conditions (learning resources, school quality), and physical conditions (green space) may foster children's cognitive skill development; policy should target multiple neighborhood dimensions simultaneously rather than single-factor interventions. and green space to academic skills.
reviewer_notes: For academic skills, children tended to score lower in reading and math when they lived in neighborhoods with more violent crime or higher pollution. They scored higher when their neighborhoods offered more learning resources, when local schools had stronger average achievement, and when there was more green space. Concentrated disadvantage and the share of students enrolled in AP courses were not related to reading or math once the fixed effects were included. For executive functions, higher neighborhood pollution predicted poorer executive functioning, while higher school-level AP enrollment predicted better executive functioning. The other neighborhood characteristics showed no clear association with executive function in the fixed effects models.
